beats.script_body: In 1658, a group of Dutch farmers settled in northern Manhattan, in a landscape that reminded them of the Holland town of Haarlem. They christened their new settlement 'Nieuw Haarlem' — then a distant nine miles from New York City, which clustered around the southern tip of the island. The name was Anglicized after Dutch rule ceded to the British in 1664. During the eighteenth century, elite New Yorkers established country estates and working farms here; one such estate belonged to Alexander Hamilton, who gave his name to the neighborhood of Hamilton Heights, and whose home, Hamilton Grange, still stands as a monument to the area's colonial past.

beats.script_body: The extension of the subway up Lenox Avenue in 1904 set off a wave of speculative building in Harlem, especially above 130th Street. Real estate developers overbuilt — and simply could not fill their properties. That depressed market coincided with a major influx of African Americans to New York. Southern blacks, fleeing racial violence and seeking economic opportunity, migrated en masse to northern cities, while African Americans were being squeezed out of their neighborhoods on the west side of Midtown. For years, white developers, pressured by white Harlemites, had refused to rent or sell to blacks. But empty buildings and the urging of black entrepreneurs eventually convinced them to change their policies, and in the first decade of the twentieth century the Harlem housing market was opened to blacks. When efforts to stem the tide of black in-migration failed, most white Harlemites moved out. By the 1920s, Harlem above 125th Street was the undisputed capital of Afro-America — home to its political institutions, its legendary nightlife, and the outpouring of arts and letters known as the Harlem Renaissance.

beats.script_body: Listen to the street names around you. After the civil rights movement of the 1960s, many of Harlem's streets were renamed to honor prominent African Americans. Eighth Avenue became Frederick Douglass Boulevard; Seventh Avenue became Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard; and Sixth Avenue, originally named Lenox Avenue, became Malcolm X Boulevard — while 125th Street was renamed for Martin Luther King, Jr. The old names and the new names still coexist on signs and in conversation throughout the neighborhood.

beats.script_body: The row of tenement houses at Nos. 107-145 on the north side of the street was built in 1905 for middle-class and ambitious working-class whites, but the early-century real estate depression left many apartments vacant, and the owner refused to rent to African Americans. When St. Philip's Episcopal Church, a black congregation from the Tenderloin, decided to move to Harlem in 1911, it bought these tenements. Its pastor, the Reverend Hutchens Bishop — a light-skinned man — was able to purchase the real estate because the developers who sold it to him thought he was white. With that transaction, the color line west of Lenox Avenue was broken, paving the way for the development of Black Harlem.

beats.script_body: This intersection of 135th Street and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard was the institutional hub of Harlem during the 1920s and 1930s. Within a stone's throw, one could find the headquarters of the NAACP, the National Urban League, and Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association. Close by were the offices of the major black newspapers — the conservative Amsterdam News and the more militant New York Age — along with the New York Public Library and the YMCA. By 1920, Harlem had become New York's primary African American neighborhood, and most black political and social institutions had moved here.

beats.script_body: The YMCA at 181 West 135th Street was founded in 1851 to give moral and spiritual guidance to young male migrants from rural areas — but its membership and outreach were restricted to white men until 1867. A 'colored men's branch' opened on West Fifty-third Street in 1900 to serve migrants from the South, and moved to this location in 1919. Demand was so great that an annex was built across the street in 1932. This branch also served as a hotel for black visitors denied access to the segregated hotels elsewhere in the city.

beats.script_body: During the Harlem Renaissance, the literati met inside this YMCA to exchange ideas — among its guests were Ralph Ellison, Langston Hughes, and James Baldwin. The Y's Little Theater program launched the careers of actors such as Sidney Poitier, Eartha Kitt, Cicely Tyson, and Danny Glover. Other patrons who went on to prominence included Jackie Robinson, Richard Wright, Paul Robeson, Jesse Owens, Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson, and Willie Mays.

beats.script_body: On the southwest corner of 135th Street, at 2294½ Adam Clayton Powell, Jr. Boulevard — now an empty building — stood Ed Small's Paradise, one of Harlem's most popular jazz clubs and restaurants from the 1920s to the 1940s. Those who could afford the prices at the 'Hottest Spot in Harlem' were treated to music, elaborate floor shows, and singing waiters. The dance floor got so crowded that each patron was said to have a dime's worth of floor space for dancing. A young Malcolm Little, after losing his job as a waiter here, began a downward spiral into criminality that eventually landed him in jail — where he converted to Islam and changed his name to Malcolm X. In the 1960s, basketball star Wilt Chamberlain reopened the restaurant as Big Wilt's Small's Paradise.

beats.script_body: Across the street stood 220 West 135th Street, the former home of Florence Mills, one of the most popular singers and dancers of the 1920s. An international star, Mills performed on Broadway and abroad. Hoping that her success would make 'people think better of other colored folk,' she passed over an offer to perform in the Ziegfeld Follies in order to join an all-black revue, paving the way for entertainers like Josephine Baker. She died of appendicitis in 1927, at the age of thirty-one. Her funeral was the largest in Harlem's history: more than 5,000 mourners filled Harlem's Mother Zion AME Church, and more than 150,000 followed the funeral cortege through the streets. At the cemetery, a low-flying plane released a flock of blackbirds as a final goodbye.

beats.script_body: Right next door, 224 West 135th Street — now Flo's Beauty Salon — was the former headquarters of the NAACP. Formed in 1909, the interracial organization fought through judicial and legislative channels for voting rights, integration, and equal opportunity. Its monthly publication, The Crisis, edited by W. E. B. Du Bois from 1909 to 1934, had a circulation of more than one hundred thousand by 1920. The NAACP's Legal Defense and Education Fund, established in 1939, would go on to try the landmark Brown v. Board of Education case of 1954: Legal Director Thurgood Marshall's argument before the Supreme Court led to nationwide school integration and sparked the legal phase of the civil rights movement. In 1965, Marshall became the first African American justice appointed to the United States Supreme Court.

beats.script_body: One of the most important literary sites on this block, 267 West 136th Street, is now a parking lot. During the 1920s, this boarding house was occupied entirely by the vanguard wing of the Harlem Renaissance: Zora Neale Hurston, Langston Hughes, painters Bruce Nugent and Aaron Douglas, and novelist Wallace Thurman — the de facto leader of the radical group — all called '267 House' home. Far more interested in bohemian themes than racial ones, Thurman resisted the idea that African American artists had to represent their race in their art, and mocked the Renaissance leaders who believed civil rights would be won through cultural production. Thurman and Hurston called such figures 'the Niggerati,' and the radical residents self-deprecatingly nicknamed their boarding home 'Niggerati Manor.'

beats.script_body: The Harlem Renaissance was not a spontaneous burst of artistic expression — in many ways it was a political movement. Black intellectuals such as W. E. B. Du Bois, Charles Johnson, and Alain Locke promoted the notion that African Americans could gain equality and respect through arts and letters; when white Americans saw the cultural contributions of African Americans, they argued, they would naturally see blacks as their equals. The stakes were high in the 1920s, a nadir in American race relations: lynching was epidemic, and the summer of 1919 saw so many bloody anti-black riots across the country that it became known as the 'Red Summer.' Civil rights organizations joined black and white philanthropists in funding the work; The Crisis and Opportunity, the magazines of the NAACP and Urban League, sponsored literary contests. Yet while the writers and artists were black, the publishers and patrons were almost entirely white — a dichotomy that led many to argue the Renaissance catered to a 'white' view of black aesthetic forms.

beats.script_body: For a brief period in the 1930s, 239 West 136th Street was the headquarters of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. At the time, virtually all railroad porters were black men, for whom these jobs were high-status positions leading to a middle-class lifestyle. Led by A. Philip Randolph, the Brotherhood was the nation's first African American labor union, and its most significant campaign was its struggle — won finally in 1937 — to gain official recognition from the Pullman Company.

beats.script_body: The area bounded by 138th and 139th Streets and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., and Frederick Douglass Boulevards is the St. Nicholas Historic District. Originally the King Model Houses, these brownstones and apartment buildings were the project of developer David H. King, who in 1890 bought the large plot from the Equitable Life Assurance Company and commissioned three prominent architectural firms to design affordable, attractive homes for white middle-class New Yorkers. The result is some of the loveliest residential streets in the city — and the alleys running between and behind the buildings, where garbage and delivery vehicles are diverted, are a rarity in New York, leaving the streets relatively free of congestion, noise, and dirt.

beats.script_body: Because of the economic depression of the 1890s, King managed to sell only nine of the 146 rowhouses and three apartment buildings before Equitable foreclosed in 1895 and took over. In the 1920s, after restricting them to whites for years, Equitable began selling the buildings to African Americans. Some black professionals bought homes here, but most owners were members of the black working class — laundresses, railroad porters, hairdressers, domestic servants, elevator operators — who converted many of the homes into rooming houses. During this period the streets became known as 'Strivers' Row,' reflecting the ambition of those who managed to reside here. As you walk, notice the signs on the gateposts still asking you to 'Walk Your Horses.'

beats.script_body: You are standing at the eastern edge of Sugar Hill. If Strivers' Row was for those working hard to make it, Sugar Hill was for those who had succeeded. Its exquisite rowhouses and apartment buildings were originally occupied by white professionals, but as the boundaries of Black Harlem pushed outward, whites fled and wealthy blacks moved in. 'Sugar' was slang for money, found in abundance here, and it gave the neighborhood its nickname in the 1920s. Wealthy denizens included Lena Horne, socialite A'Lelia Walker Robinson, and NAACP officers W. E. B. Du Bois, Walter White, Thurgood Marshall, and Roy Wilkins. In the 1980s, the rap band the Sugarhill Gang made the neighborhood a household name with 'Rapper's Delight,' the first rap song to cross over to the pop charts. Sugar Hill is part of Hamilton Heights, once the country estate of Alexander Hamilton.

beats.script_body: Looking west and up the hill from the corner, you'll notice an impressive Gothic building with white trim. This is Shepard Hall, the main building of the City College of New York, one of the nineteen colleges of the City University of New York system. Established in 1847 as the Free Academy, CCNY has historically provided educational opportunities for immigrant workers and their children; after World War I it gained a reputation for excellence and was known for a time as the 'People's Harvard.' When CCNY moved to this location in 1902, the city was building the subway system, and the Manhattan schist excavated for it — the bedrock of Manhattan Island — was used to construct Shepard Hall and other CCNY buildings.

beats.script_body: On the southeast corner — formerly 2341-2359 Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard — stood the original Renaissance Theater, Ballroom, and Casino, known locally as 'the Renny.' From the 1920s to the 1950s it was one of Harlem's most popular nightclubs, and it was home to the Rennies, the nation's first all-black professional basketball team, founded in 1923. Professional basketball was segregated in the early twentieth century, but the Rennies were known during the 1930s as the best team in the world. When they stopped playing in 1940, they had an astounding record of 2,558 wins and only 592 losses.

beats.script_body: At 136-142 West 138th Street stands Abyssinian Baptist Church, one of the oldest and largest Protestant churches in the United States. In 1808, a group of free blacks protesting segregated seating in the First Baptist Church of New York City formed Abyssinian together with a group of Ethiopian merchants. After homes on Worth Street, Waverly Place, and West Fortieth Street, the Reverend Adam Clayton Powell Sr., pastor from 1908, raised money to move the church to this location in 1920. By 1937, when Powell turned the pulpit over to his son Adam Clayton Powell Jr., the congregation had seven thousand members, making it the largest Protestant congregation in the country. Powell Jr. continued his father's civil rights tradition, serving as pastor while becoming the first African American congressman, representing Harlem in the U.S. House from 1944 to 1970.

beats.script_body: In the 1920s, 120 West 138th Street was the site of Liberty Hall, the Harlem headquarters of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association. A flamboyant and extremely popular figure who arrived from Jamaica in 1917, Garvey reminds us of the central role West Indian immigrants played in Harlem life. Initially influenced by Booker T. Washington's self-help doctrines, Garvey became a proponent of black pride and pan-Africanism. The UNIA appealed, unlike other civil rights organizations, to the Southern migrants and Caribbean immigrants who made up the black working class; its Harlem branch, the country's largest, had more than forty thousand members. Garvey's stance made him enemies among other black leaders, including A. Philip Randolph and W. E. B. Du Bois. Arrested on trumped-up charges of mail fraud in 1923 and convicted in 1927, he was deported to Jamaica — but he left a strong legacy that would influence the black nationalist movements of the 1960s and 1970s.

beats.source_passage: In the 1920s, 120 West 138th Street was the site of Liberty Hall, the Harlem headquarters of Marcus Garvey’s Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Garvey was a flamboyant, charismatic, and extremely popular figure who arrived in New York from Jamaica in 1917. Initially influenced by the self-help doctrines and racial accommodationist stance of Booker T. Washington, Garvey became a proponent of black pride and pan-Africanism. The UNIA, an international organization, had a huge national membership, appealing, unlike other civil rights organizations, to the Southern migrants and Caribbean immigrants who made up the black working class. The Harlem branch of the UNIA, the country’s largest, had more than forty thousand members. Garvey’s political activities and stance made him enemies among other black leaders, including A. Philip Randolph, James Weldon Johnson, and W. E. B. Du Bois. Arrested on trumped-up charges of mail fraud in 1923, Garvey was convicted in 1927. His subsequent deportation to Jamaica effectively ended his activities in the United States. But Garvey left a strong legacy behind and would eventually prove a major influence on the black nationalist movements of the 1960s and 1970s.

beats.script_body: Lenox Avenue was the site of all the major parades through Harlem in the early twentieth century. In July 1917, W. E. B. Du Bois, James Weldon Johnson, and other NAACP officers led ten thousand people down the avenue in a solemn protest march. Three weeks before, in East St. Louis, Illinois, nearly two hundred African Americans had died and six thousand had been burned out of their homes in the worst race riot in American history. The Harlem protesters walked in silence, bearing signs that read 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' and 'Mr. President, Why Not Make America Safe for Democracy?' The hypocrisy of a government fighting a war abroad in the name of liberty while refusing civil rights at home led many African Americans to question whether they should participate in World War I.

beats.script_body: Black Americans did fight in World War I, and the 369th Regiment, an all-black unit from Harlem, became the most highly decorated American unit and the only one awarded the French croix de guerre. Known as the 'Harlem Hellfighters,' the 369th returned home triumphantly in February 1919 to a parade through Manhattan; when they crossed 110th Street and turned onto Lenox Avenue, the parade became a party as they were greeted by friends, family, and great cheers. Black soldiers had found better treatment abroad than at home, and many returned with a more militant stance — the 'New Negro' that Alain Locke would name in his 1925 essay.

beats.script_body: The Countee Cullen Branch of the New York Public Library, at 104 West 136th, stands on the site of the former home of Madame C. J. Walker, the richest self-made woman in early twentieth-century America. Born in the South, Walker made her fortune developing and selling hair straighteners, skin lighteners, and other beauty products for African American women. In 1916, already wealthy, she moved to New York and built a home, beauty salon, and school here. She was active in politics and civil rights too, leading a delegation of women to see President Woodrow Wilson to protest segregation in the military, and giving significant sums to charities and civil rights organizations.

beats.script_body: Walker's daughter, A'Lelia Walker Robinson, was famous for her lavish lifestyle and elaborate parties, hosting salons for literary figures of the Harlem Renaissance. At perhaps her most legendary party, she served African Americans caviar and champagne while whites, seated at a separate table, received chit'lins and bathtub gin. In 1927 she converted one floor of this home into the 'Dark Tower,' a coffeehouse where artists could gather — but it filled so quickly with wealthy and prominent New Yorkers that the bohemians it was meant for could barely fit, and the prices were out of their reach. Langston Hughes claimed that, more than any other event, her death in 1931 marked the end of the Harlem Renaissance.

beats.poi_name: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture
beats.script_body: On the northwest corner of 135th and Lenox stands the New York Public Library's Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, the premier research library for black history and culture. Arturo Schomburg, a Puerto Rican black, spent his life amassing a huge collection of books, pamphlets, manuscripts, and visual materials pertaining to the African and African American past. He began the endeavor in response to an elementary school teacher who claimed blacks had produced nothing worth studying — and proved him wrong. When the New York Public Library purchased Schomburg's collection in 1926, it held five thousand items; it now has over five million. Schomburg himself played a major role in the Harlem Renaissance, sponsoring readings and literary salons and serving as curator of his collection for the library.

beats.script_body: You are standing on an important speakers' corner for soapbox orators of the early twentieth century. Legend has it that Marcus Garvey, on arriving in Harlem, stole the soapbox here from A. Philip Randolph; both men were frequently seen and heard at this corner, which was also the first view of Harlem for most Southern migrants — from Penn Station, they took the IRT to 135th and Lenox and exited the subway into another world. If they craved a reminder of home, they could stop at the stand of Pig Foot Mary on the southeast corner. Born Lillian Harris, she sold Southern-style comfort food like pig's feet and chit'lins; starting with three dollars and a folding table, Harris eventually made enough to become a major real estate investor and Harlem philanthropist.

beats.script_body: The block of 133rd Street between Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard and Lenox Avenue was known in the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s as 'Jungle Alley.' Here, downtown whites attracted to Harlem nightlife could live out exoticized fantasies of black culture — scantily clad women gyrating on stage to heavy percussion amid jungle decor. Many clubs, such as the Cotton Club and Connie's Inn, both since demolished, refused service to blacks, including the very entertainers who performed on their stages. But most clubs along Jungle Alley catered to a mixed clientele, and unlike the Cotton Club and Connie's, some were owned by black proprietors. Still, they all sold a white-inspired view of a primitive, exotic Black America that bore little resemblance to the reality at neighborhood joints like Small's Paradise and the Renny.

beats.script_body: Williams Christian Methodist Church, at 2225 on the east side of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard, is the former site of the Lafayette Theater. Opened in 1912, the Lafayette was one of the few integrated theaters in New York City and one of the few venues where blacks could perform in serious roles. During the 1930s it became the Harlem headquarters of the New Deal's Federal Theater Project, whose most notorious production was the 'Voodoo Macbeth' — directed by Orson Welles with an all-black cast, integrating African elements into the Shakespeare classic.

beats.script_body: Look south toward 125th Street: the sculpture on the median of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard symbolizes the 'Tree of Hope.' The original tree, which stood in front of the Lafayette, was rumored to have magical powers, bringing employment to out-of-work actors who rubbed its bark. It became a real gathering place — casting agents looking for entertainers could find them in droves in front of the Lafayette — so the tree did, in a sense, fulfill its promise. The original oak was cut down in 1934, and this interpretive sculpture was erected in 1972. A piece of the original remains on the stage of the Apollo Theater, where amateur-night performers rub its bark for luck before going on.

beats.source_passage: The sculpture on the median in the center of the boulevard symbolizes the “Tree of Hope.” The tree, which sat in front of the Lafayette, was rumored to have magical powers, bringing employment to out-of-work actors who rubbed its bark. The old oak did become a gathering place for actors; casting agents in search of entertainers could find them in droves in front of the Lafayette, so in a sense the tree fulfilled its magic promises. The original Tree of Hope was cut down in 1934; this interpretive sculpture was erected in 1972. A piece of the original remains a fixture on the stage of the Apollo Theater, participants in Wednesday’s amateur nights rub its bark for luck before going out on stage.

beats.script_body: You are in Harlem's central commercial district. In the early twentieth century, black-owned businesses clustered around 135th Street, but on 125th, all the stores were white-owned. The owners resisted Harlem's development as a black neighborhood and most refused to hire black workers through the 1930s, even though their clientele was almost entirely black. Even today, few of the businesses on 125th Street are owned by African Americans. In the 1960s, banks and insurance companies 'red-lined' the area, refusing to lend to anyone wanting to open a business in Harlem. Given that history, many community leaders welcomed the influx of major corporations to 125th Street in the 1990s — Pathmark, the first large supermarket to open in Harlem, along with Starbucks, Old Navy, and Harlem USA, a mall and movie multiplex backed by basketball star Magic Johnson. Some feared the impact of this corporate invasion; many welcomed the lower prices, jobs, and renewed confidence in the neighborhood's future.

beats.script_body: The tall white building on the southwest corner of 125th Street and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., Boulevard is the landmarked Hotel Theresa, now an office building. When it opened in 1913 it catered to a white-only clientele, but in 1937 a black entrepreneur bought it and overturned the segregationist policies. Because posh downtown hotels refused service to blacks, the Theresa became known as the 'Waldorf of Harlem.' In 1960, Fidel Castro, in town to visit the United Nations, stayed here to show solidarity with black Americans. The hotel also housed political organizations: A. Philip Randolph's 1941 March on Washington movement was coordinated here, pushing President Franklin Roosevelt to integrate defense industries during World War II, and in the 1960s, after his break from the Nation of Islam, Malcolm X established the Organization of Afro-American Unity at the Theresa — gathering crowds outside the building to hear him speak.

beats.script_body: The old Blumstein's Department Store at 230 West 125th Street — now subdivided into smaller ground-level stores — once refused, like most stores on the block, to hire black workers in any but the most lowly positions, despite an almost entirely African American clientele. That was especially galling during the Great Depression, when Harlem's unemployment far exceeded the rest of the city's. In 1934, Adam Clayton Powell Jr. and other black leaders targeted Blumstein's in a boycott and picketing campaign under the slogan 'Don't buy where you can't work,' eventually forcing the largest department store in Harlem to hire black clerks. In time, Blumstein's would be the first department store to have a black Santa Claus.

beats.script_body: Stop at the Apollo Theater at 253 West 125th Street. The burlesque house that opened here in 1914 initially refused admission to blacks, but in 1934 the former owners of the Lafayette Theater bought the Apollo and integrated it. It has since become the premier showcase of black talent in the United States — virtually every black American entertainer of note has performed on its stage. In the 1930s and 1940s audiences enjoyed dancer Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson; singers Bessie Smith, Billie Holiday, and Ethel Waters; and bandleaders such as Duke Ellington backed by costumed chorus girls. Wednesday amateur nights, an Apollo tradition since the 1930s and televised nationally since the early 1990s, have discovered greats like Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, and James Brown. But the notoriously tough Apollo audience is no sure predictor: multiple-Grammy-winner Lauryn Hill was booed off the stage.

beats.script_body: Before there was an English presence in New York, there was an African one: Dutch settlers brought African slaves to New Amsterdam as early as 1644. As late as 1760 the city had the highest number of blacks of any urban area in the colonies, and people of African descent made up at least 15 percent of the population before the Revolutionary War. As the center of population moved up Manhattan, African Americans were pushed to the periphery, forming one 'Little Africa' after another — in the Wall Street area, Greenwich Village, the Tenderloin in the West Thirties, and San Juan Hill in the West Fifties. The mechanization of Southern agriculture, antiblack violence, and roughly forty thousand West Indian immigrants in the 1920s swelled New York's black population from about 60,000 in 1900 to over 320,000 by 1930. Landlords' greed eventually trumped their racism: recognizing they could charge African Americans well above market value, they opened Harlem's empty buildings, and by 1920, 70 percent of New York City's blacks lived in Harlem.
